subject: physics

items.q: A body moves along a straight line, with positive taken to the right. At one instant its velocity is −3.0 m s⁻¹ and its acceleration is +2.0 m s⁻². The acceleration stays constant. Which describes the motion of the body?
items.correct: Moving left and slowing down; later it will move off to the right.
items.misconception: Moving left and slowing down; it will then stop and stay at rest.
items.why: In everyday experience slowing down usually ends in stopping (a car braking, a ball rolling to rest) because the cause of the deceleration stops acting once the body is at rest. Students carry this over to cases, such as a vertical throw, where the acceleration keeps acting. If the acceleration is still acting at the instant the velocity is zero, the velocity keeps changing. A ball thrown upwards has zero velocity at the top for only an instant and then moves down; the same equations of motion, with a consistent sign convention, describe the whole motion.
items.specStatementText: that the motion of bodies through space and time can be described and analysed in terms of position, velocity, and acceleration
items.random_wrong: Moving left and speeding up, since its acceleration is positive.

items.q: A ball is thrown vertically upwards. Fluid resistance is negligible and upwards is taken as positive. Which statement about the ball at the instant it reaches its highest point is correct?
items.correct: Its velocity is zero; its acceleration is g downwards.
items.misconception: Its velocity is zero, so its acceleration is zero as well.
items.why: Students do not separate a quantity from its rate of change: velocity and acceleration are both learned as 'how fast', and a body that is not moving seems to have nothing happening to it. This velocity–acceleration confusion is one of the most widely reported findings in kinematics education research. Acceleration depends on how the velocity is changing, not on its value. At the highest point of a vertical throw the velocity passes from upwards to downwards, so it is changing at g even though it is momentarily zero.
items.specStatementText: velocity is the rate of change of position, and acceleration is the rate of change of velocity
items.random_wrong: Its acceleration is reversing from upwards to downwards.

items.q: A graph of velocity against time for a trolley moving along a straight track is a straight line from (0 s, 1.0 m s⁻¹) to (2.0 s, 4.0 m s⁻¹). What is the acceleration of the trolley at t = 2.0 s?
items.correct: 1.5 m s⁻²
items.misconception: 2.0 m s⁻²
items.why:
At GCSE many examples start from rest, where a = v/t gives the right answer, so the formula is remembered without the initial velocity. It is reinforced by reading the units m s⁻² as 'metres per second per second'. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity: a = Δv/Δt = (v − u)/t. For a body that starts at 1.0 m s⁻¹ and reaches 4.0 m s⁻¹ in 2.0 s, the change is 3.0 m s⁻¹, so a = 1.5 m s⁻², not 4.0/2.0.

Working: Acceleration = gradient of the velocity–time graph. The graph is a straight line, so the acceleration is uniform and equals the gradient at every instant, including t = 2.0 s: a = Δv/Δt = (4.0 − 1.0) m s⁻¹ / (2.0 − 0) s = 3.0 m s⁻¹ / 2.0 s = 1.5 m s⁻².
items.specStatementText: velocity is the rate of change of position, and acceleration is the rate of change of velocity
items.random_wrong: 5.0 m s⁻²
items.working: Acceleration = gradient of the velocity–time graph. The graph is a straight line, so the acceleration is uniform and equals the gradient at every instant, including t = 2.0 s: a = Δv/Δt = (4.0 − 1.0) m s⁻¹ / (2.0 − 0) s = 3.0 m s⁻¹ / 2.0 s = 1.5 m s⁻².

items.q: A runner moves along a straight track. Her position x is measured from a marker on the track. She starts at x = +30 m, runs to x = +70 m, then turns round and runs to x = −20 m, where she stops. What is her displacement?
items.why:
In everyday use 'how far did you go' means the distance travelled, and in many introductory problems the body moves in one direction so the two values coincide. Students therefore treat the words as synonyms. Distance adds up every part of the path; displacement depends only on the start and end positions. A runner completing one lap of a track travels 400 m but has zero displacement.

Working: Displacement = x(final) − x(initial) = (−20 m) − (+30 m) = −50 m, i.e. 50 m in the negative direction. (Distance travelled = (70 − 30) m + (70 − (−20)) m = 40 m + 90 m = 130 m.)
items.specStatementText: the change in position is the displacement
items.working: Displacement = x(final) − x(initial) = (−20 m) − (+30 m) = −50 m, i.e. 50 m in the negative direction. (Distance travelled = (70 − 30) m + (70 − (−20)) m = 40 m + 90 m = 130 m.)

items.q: A body moves from point P to point Q. Which statement about its displacement is correct?
items.correct: Its magnitude can be less than the distance travelled, but never greater.
items.misconception: It depends on the route taken, whereas the distance does not.
items.why: In everyday English 'the distance between two towns' means how far apart they are, and phrases such as 'as the crow flies' reinforce it, so students attach the straight-line meaning to 'distance' and the route-dependent meaning to the unfamiliar word 'displacement'. Distance depends on the route and is a scalar. Displacement is the vector from start to finish and does not depend on the route. A round trip has a non-zero distance and zero displacement.
items.specStatementText: the difference between distance and displacement
items.random_wrong: It equals the total length of the path followed from P to Q.

items.q: A car travels 3.0 km along a straight road at a constant speed of 10 m s⁻¹, then returns along the same road to its starting point at a constant speed of 15 m s⁻¹. What are its average speed and its average velocity for the whole journey?
items.correct: Average speed 12 m s⁻¹; average velocity 0 m s⁻¹
items.misconception: Average speed 12.5 m s⁻¹; average velocity 0 m s⁻¹
items.why:
'Average' in mathematics means the arithmetic mean, so students apply that procedure to speeds. It gives the right answer in the common textbook case of equal time intervals, which reinforces it. Use the definition: average speed = total distance ÷ total time. When equal distances are covered at different speeds, more time is spent at the lower speed, so the average speed is less than the mean of the two speeds.

Working: Time out = 3000 m ÷ 10 m s⁻¹ = 300 s; time back = 3000 m ÷ 15 m s⁻¹ = 200 s; total time = 500 s. Average speed = total distance ÷ total time = 6000 m ÷ 500 s = 12 m s⁻¹. The car ends at its starting point, so displacement = 0 and average velocity = 0 ÷ 500 s = 0 m s⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: the difference between instantaneous and average values of velocity, speed and acceleration, and how to determine them
items.random_wrong: Average speed 12 m s⁻¹; average velocity 12 m s⁻¹
items.working: Time out = 3000 m ÷ 10 m s⁻¹ = 300 s; time back = 3000 m ÷ 15 m s⁻¹ = 200 s; total time = 500 s. Average speed = total distance ÷ total time = 6000 m ÷ 500 s = 12 m s⁻¹. The car ends at its starting point, so displacement = 0 and average velocity = 0 ÷ 500 s = 0 m s⁻¹.

items.q: A car starts from rest at t = 0 and x = 0 and moves along a straight road. A graph of its position x against time t is a curve that gets steeper with time. At t = 3.0 s, x = 16.5 m, and the tangent to the curve at this point also passes through the point (5.0 s, 40.5 m). What is the instantaneous velocity of the car at t = 3.0 s?
items.correct: 12 m s⁻¹
items.misconception: 5.5 m s⁻¹
items.why:
The GCSE relation 'speed = distance ÷ time' is learned for constant speed, where average and instantaneous values are the same. Students keep using it when the speed is changing. For an accelerating body, Δx/Δt over an interval gives the average velocity (the gradient of the chord). The instantaneous velocity is the gradient of the tangent; for a body accelerating uniformly from rest it is twice the average velocity.

Working: Instantaneous velocity = gradient of the tangent to the position–time graph at t = 3.0 s. The tangent passes through (3.0 s, 16.5 m) and (5.0 s, 40.5 m): v = (40.5 − 16.5) m / (5.0 − 3.0) s = 24 m / 2.0 s = 12 m s⁻¹. (For comparison, the average velocity over the first 3.0 s is 16.5 m / 3.0 s = 5.5 m s⁻¹.)
items.specStatementText: the difference between instantaneous and average values of velocity, speed and acceleration, and how to determine them
items.working: Instantaneous velocity = gradient of the tangent to the position–time graph at t = 3.0 s. The tangent passes through (3.0 s, 16.5 m) and (5.0 s, 40.5 m): v = (40.5 − 16.5) m / (5.0 − 3.0) s = 24 m / 2.0 s = 12 m s⁻¹. (For comparison, the average velocity over the first 3.0 s is 16.5 m / 3.0 s = 5.5 m s⁻¹.)

items.q: A car travelling at 16 m s⁻¹ brakes with uniform deceleration and comes to rest in 4.0 s. What distance does the car travel while braking?
items.why:
The GCSE relation distance = speed × time is learned for constant speed and is the most familiar motion equation, so it is used whenever a speed and a time are given. For changing speed, use the average speed (for uniform acceleration, (u + v)/2) or the area under the velocity–time graph. The initial or final speed alone gives the wrong distance.

Working: u = 16 m s⁻¹, v = 0, t = 4.0 s, acceleration uniform. s = ((u + v)/2)t = ((16 + 0)/2 m s⁻¹)(4.0 s) = 32 m. Check: a = (v − u)/t = (0 − 16)/4.0 = −4.0 m s⁻²; s = ut + ½at² = (16)(4.0) + ½(−4.0)(4.0)² = 64 − 32 = 32 m.
items.specStatementText: the equations of motion for solving problems with uniformly accelerated motion as given by s = ((u + v)/2)t; v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as

items.q: A stone is released from rest and falls 5.00 m. Fluid resistance is negligible. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². What is the speed of the stone when it has fallen 5.00 m?
items.why:
Students rearrange for v² or t² and then write down the calculator display, forgetting the final step. The error is most common once the square has been isolated on one side, because the working then looks finished. Finish the rearrangement: v = √(u² + 2as) and, from rest, t = √(2s/a). Check the units: m² s⁻² is the unit of v², not v.

Working: Take downwards as positive: u = 0, s = 5.00 m, a = 9.8 m s⁻². v² = u² + 2as = 0 + 2(9.8 m s⁻²)(5.00 m) = 98.0 m² s⁻², so v = √98.0 = 9.90 m s⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: the equations of motion for solving problems with uniformly accelerated motion as given by s = ((u + v)/2)t; v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as
items.working: Take downwards as positive: u = 0, s = 5.00 m, a = 9.8 m s⁻². v² = u² + 2as = 0 + 2(9.8 m s⁻²)(5.00 m) = 98.0 m² s⁻², so v = √98.0 = 9.90 m s⁻¹.

items.q: Which statement about when the equations of motion s = ((u + v)/2)t, v = u + at, s = ut + ½at² and v² = u² + 2as can be applied is correct?
items.correct: They apply whenever the acceleration is constant in size and direction.
items.misconception: They apply to any straight-line motion, even if the acceleration varies.
items.why: Textbook problems for these equations are almost all in a straight line, so students remember 'straight line' as the condition and forget 'constant acceleration'. Check that the acceleration is constant before choosing an equation of motion. If it varies, use the motion graphs instead: the displacement is the area under the velocity–time graph and the acceleration is its gradient.
items.specStatementText: the equations of motion for solving problems with uniformly accelerated motion as given by s = ((u + v)/2)t; v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as
items.random_wrong: They apply to a skydiver falling through air, as g is constant.

items.q: A car starts from rest and moves along a straight road. Its acceleration is greatest at the start and decreases continuously, falling quickly at first and then more slowly, but stays positive, until the car reaches 20 m s⁻¹ at t = 10 s. Which gives the distance travelled by the car in these 10 s?
items.correct: Between 100 m and 200 m, since its speed rises fastest early on
items.misconception: Exactly 100 m, as its average velocity is (0 + 20)/2 m s⁻¹
items.why:
The equation s = ((u + v)/2)t is learned without its condition, and the arithmetic mean feels like the natural meaning of 'average'. (u + v)/2 is the average velocity only when the velocity–time graph is a straight line. For a curved graph, find the displacement from the area under the graph and divide by the time.

Working: Displacement = area under the velocity–time graph. Uniform acceleration from 0 to 20 m s⁻¹ in 10 s would give a straight line with area ½ × 10 s × 20 m s⁻¹ = 100 m. With the acceleration greatest at the start and decreasing, the graph is a curve that rises steeply then flattens, lying above that straight line, so the area exceeds 100 m. The acceleration is positive throughout, so the velocity is below 20 m s⁻¹ before t = 10 s and the area is less than 20 m s⁻¹ × 10 s = 200 m. So 100 m < distance < 200 m.
items.specStatementText: motion with uniform and non-uniform acceleration
items.random_wrong: Exactly 200 m, as it moves at 20 m s⁻¹ for the whole 10 s
items.working: Displacement = area under the velocity–time graph. Uniform acceleration from 0 to 20 m s⁻¹ in 10 s would give a straight line with area ½ × 10 s × 20 m s⁻¹ = 100 m. With the acceleration greatest at the start and decreasing, the graph is a curve that rises steeply then flattens, lying above that straight line, so the area exceeds 100 m. The acceleration is positive throughout, so the velocity is below 20 m s⁻¹ before t = 10 s and the area is less than 20 m s⁻¹ × 10 s = 200 m. So 100 m < distance < 200 m.

items.q: A graph of velocity against time for a sprinter starts at the origin, rises steeply, becomes gradually less steep, and is a horizontal line at 11 m s⁻¹ from t = 6.0 s until the end of the race. Which describes the sprinter's motion?
items.correct: The acceleration falls to zero while the speed rises to a steady value.
items.misconception: The acceleration decreases, so the sprinter is slowing down after the start.
items.why: Students conflate acceleration with velocity, so a fall in one is read as a fall in the other. The everyday word 'decelerate' reinforces the link between 'less acceleration' and 'slower'. A body slows down only when its acceleration is opposite to its velocity. A sprinter whose acceleration is decreasing but still forwards keeps getting faster until the acceleration reaches zero.
items.specStatementText: motion with uniform and non-uniform acceleration
items.random_wrong: The acceleration increases, since the sprinter keeps getting faster.

items.q: A ball is kicked horizontally at 12 m s⁻¹ from the top of a vertical cliff 20 m high and lands on level ground below. Fluid resistance is negligible. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². How far from the foot of the cliff does the ball land?
items.why:
Students treat the equations of motion as one-dimensional recipes and substitute the only speed given in the question, without seeing that the motion has two independent components. Failure to treat the components separately is a documented difficulty in projectile problems. Resolve first: u_x = u cos θ and u_y = u sin θ (u_y = 0 for a horizontal launch). Use only u_y with g in the vertical equations and only u_x in the horizontal ones.

Working: Take downwards as positive. Vertical: u_y = 0, s = 20 m, a = 9.8 m s⁻²; s = ½at² gives t = √(2s/a) = √(40/9.8) = 2.02 s. Horizontal: u_x = 12 m s⁻¹ constant (no horizontal acceleration), so x = u_x t = (12 m s⁻¹)(2.02 s) = 24 m.
items.specStatementText: the behaviour of projectiles in the absence of fluid resistance, and the application of the equations of motion resolved into vertical and horizontal components
items.working: Take downwards as positive. Vertical: u_y = 0, s = 20 m, a = 9.8 m s⁻²; s = ½at² gives t = √(2s/a) = √(40/9.8) = 2.02 s. Horizontal: u_x = 12 m s⁻¹ constant (no horizontal acceleration), so x = u_x t = (12 m s⁻¹)(2.02 s) = 24 m.

items.q: A ball is kicked from level ground at 20.0 m s⁻¹ at 30.0° above the horizontal. Fluid resistance is negligible. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². What is the maximum height reached by the ball?
items.why:
The trigonometric ratios are memorised rather than read from a sketch, and in other problems (such as inclined planes) the angle is measured from a different line, so students swap sin and cos. Sketch the velocity triangle. The component ADJACENT to the angle θ is u cos θ; the component OPPOSITE θ is u sin θ. With θ measured from the horizontal, the horizontal component is adjacent.

Working: Vertical component of launch velocity: u_y = u sin θ = 20.0 × sin 30.0° = 10.0 m s⁻¹ (upwards positive). At maximum height v_y = 0: v_y² = u_y² − 2gh, so h = u_y²/(2g) = (10.0 m s⁻¹)² / (2 × 9.8 m s⁻²) = 5.10 m.
items.specStatementText: the behaviour of projectiles in the absence of fluid resistance, and the application of the equations of motion resolved into vertical and horizontal components
items.working: Vertical component of launch velocity: u_y = u sin θ = 20.0 × sin 30.0° = 10.0 m s⁻¹ (upwards positive). At maximum height v_y = 0: v_y² = u_y² − 2gh, so h = u_y²/(2g) = (10.0 m s⁻¹)² / (2 × 9.8 m s⁻²) = 5.10 m.

items.q: A stone is thrown from the top of a cliff at 15.0 m s⁻¹ at 30.0° below the horizontal. It lands in the sea 40.0 m below the point of release. Fluid resistance is negligible. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². How long after release does the stone reach the sea?
items.why:
The most common textbook example of a launch from a height is a horizontal launch, so 'u_y = 0' becomes attached to any cliff or table problem. Launches below the horizontal are met less often. Resolve the launch velocity every time. For a launch below the horizontal, the initial vertical velocity is u sin θ downwards, which shortens the time to reach the ground.

Working: Take downwards as positive. u_y = 15.0 × sin 30.0° = 7.50 m s⁻¹, s = 40.0 m, a = 9.8 m s⁻². s = u_y t + ½at²: 40.0 = 7.50t + 4.9t², i.e. 4.9t² + 7.50t − 40.0 = 0. t = [−7.50 + √(7.50² + 4 × 4.9 × 40.0)] / (2 × 4.9) = (−7.50 + 28.99)/9.8 = 2.19 s (the other root is negative).
items.specStatementText: the behaviour of projectiles in the absence of fluid resistance, and the application of the equations of motion resolved into vertical and horizontal components

items.q: Ball X, of mass 0.20 kg, rolls off a horizontal table top at 3.0 m s⁻¹. At the same instant ball Y, of mass 0.40 kg, is released from rest at the same height. Fluid resistance is negligible. Which ball reaches the floor first?
items.correct: They land together, as both start with zero vertical velocity.
items.misconception: Y lands first, as X's horizontal motion keeps it in the air longer.
items.why: Cartoons show characters running off cliffs and hanging in the air, and aircraft and thrown frisbees do stay up by moving through the air. Asked to predict, many students expect horizontal motion to delay falling. Gravity gives every projectile the same vertical acceleration g whatever its horizontal velocity. A ball rolling off a table and a ball dropped from the same height at the same instant land together.
items.specStatementText: the behaviour of projectiles in the absence of fluid resistance, and the application of the equations of motion resolved into vertical and horizontal components
items.random_wrong: Y lands first, as a heavier ball falls with greater acceleration.

items.q: A ball is launched at 40° above the horizontal over level ground. Fluid resistance is negligible. Which statement describes the ball at its highest point?
items.correct: Its velocity is horizontal and non-zero; its acceleration is g downwards.
items.misconception: Its velocity is momentarily zero; its acceleration is g downwards.
items.why: Students first study a ball thrown vertically upwards, which is momentarily at rest at the top, and generalise this to every projectile without separating the components. At the highest point only the vertical component of velocity is zero. The horizontal component, u cos θ, is unchanged, so the projectile is moving horizontally at that speed.
items.specStatementText: the behaviour of projectiles in the absence of fluid resistance, and the application of the equations of motion resolved into vertical and horizontal components
items.random_wrong: Its velocity is horizontal and non-zero; it has no acceleration.

items.q: A small steel ball is released from rest in air and falls until it reaches terminal speed. How does its acceleration change during this time?
items.correct: It decreases from g towards zero as the fluid resistance increases.
items.misconception: It is constant but less than g, because fluid resistance is constant.
items.why: Students meet friction first, and sliding friction is often modelled as constant; they carry the same model over to air resistance. Diagrams that show one fixed arrow labelled 'air resistance' reinforce it. Fluid resistance is zero when a body is at rest relative to the fluid and grows as its speed increases. This is why a falling body reaches terminal speed: the resistance grows until it balances the weight.
items.specStatementText: the qualitative effect of fluid resistance on projectiles, including time of flight, trajectory, velocity, acceleration, range and terminal speed.
items.random_wrong: It stays equal to g, since fluid resistance only lowers the ball's speed.

items.q: A shuttlecock is hit from ground level at 45° above the horizontal. Video analysis shows that it reaches its highest point 0.58 s after launch, at a horizontal distance of 3.6 m from the launch point, and lands 1.36 s after launch, 5.9 m from the launch point. Which conclusion do these data support?
items.correct: Fluid resistance is significant: the descent is steeper and takes longer than the ascent.
items.misconception: The data must be faulty, as a projectile's path is symmetrical about its highest point.
items.why: Students see many symmetrical parabolas in problems without fluid resistance and in mathematics, so they picture fluid resistance as shrinking the same shape rather than changing it. Fluid resistance acts against the velocity at every point and grows with speed, so the path is lopsided: the ascent is shallower and quicker, the descent steeper and slower.
items.specStatementText: the qualitative effect of fluid resistance on projectiles, including time of flight, trajectory, velocity, acceleration, range and terminal speed.
items.random_wrong: Fluid resistance cannot explain this, as it only makes the shuttlecock move more slowly.

items.q: A small plastic ball is launched without spin from level ground at 30° above the horizontal. The motion is compared with an identical launch in which fluid resistance is negligible. Which describes the effect of fluid resistance on the ball's motion?
items.correct: The range is shorter, and the horizontal velocity component decreases during the flight.
items.misconception: The range is shorter, but the horizontal velocity component stays constant in flight.
items.why: Free-fall and terminal-speed examples always draw fluid resistance as an upward arrow, and the rule 'horizontal velocity is constant' learned for projectiles without fluid resistance is carried over unchanged. Draw the fluid resistance along the velocity, pointing backwards. Resolve it: its horizontal component slows the horizontal motion at every point, which is why the range is reduced and the descent is steeper than the ascent.
items.specStatementText: the qualitative effect of fluid resistance on projectiles, including time of flight, trajectory, velocity, acceleration, range and terminal speed.
items.random_wrong: The range is shorter, and the highest point is still reached at exactly half the range.

items.q: The position x of a body moving along a straight line is recorded at intervals of 1.0 s, starting at t = 0: x = 0, 5.0 m, 8.0 m, 9.0 m, 8.0 m, 5.0 m and 0. Which statement about the motion of the body is correct?
items.correct: The acceleration is constant and negative; the body reverses direction at t = 3.0 s.
items.misconception: The acceleration is negative up to t = 3.0 s, then positive as the body speeds up again.
items.why:
In everyday English 'accelerate' means 'go faster' and 'decelerate' means 'go slower', and at GCSE a deceleration is often written as a negative acceleration for a body moving in the positive direction, so students attach 'speeding up' to the plus sign. The sign of an acceleration gives its direction relative to the chosen positive direction. Compare it with the sign of the velocity: same sign, the speed increases; opposite signs, the speed decreases. A body moving in the negative direction with a positive acceleration is slowing down.

Working: Changes in position over successive 1.0 s intervals: +5.0, +3.0, +1.0, −1.0, −3.0, −5.0 m, so the average velocities are +5.0, +3.0, +1.0, −1.0, −3.0, −5.0 m s⁻¹. Each is 2.0 m s⁻¹ less than the one before, so the acceleration is constant at −2.0 m s⁻². The velocity passes through zero at t = 3.0 s (where x = 9.0 m is greatest): the body reverses direction there while its acceleration stays −2.0 m s⁻².
items.specStatementText: that the motion of bodies through space and time can be described and analysed in terms of position, velocity, and acceleration
items.random_wrong: The acceleration is zero at t = 3.0 s, because the body is momentarily at rest at that time.
items.working: Changes in position over successive 1.0 s intervals: +5.0, +3.0, +1.0, −1.0, −3.0, −5.0 m, so the average velocities are +5.0, +3.0, +1.0, −1.0, −3.0, −5.0 m s⁻¹. Each is 2.0 m s⁻¹ less than the one before, so the acceleration is constant at −2.0 m s⁻². The velocity passes through zero at t = 3.0 s (where x = 9.0 m is greatest): the body reverses direction there while its acceleration stays −2.0 m s⁻².

items.q: A runner moves along a straight track. Observer A measures her position from a marker M, taking the direction in which she first runs as positive. Observer B measures her position from a marker N, which is 15 m from M in the positive direction, and takes the same direction as positive. According to observer A, the runner starts at +25 m, runs to +95 m, turns round, runs back to +5.0 m and stops. What is the displacement of the runner according to observer B?
items.why:
Many textbook problems start the body at the origin, so the final position and the displacement have the same value and students never need to distinguish them. The words 'position' and 'displacement' are then used interchangeably. Displacement is Δx = x(final) − x(initial). Only when the body starts at the origin does it equal the final position.

Working: According to B, positions are 15 m less than according to A: the runner starts at (25 − 15) m = +10 m and finishes at (5.0 − 15) m = −10 m. Displacement = x(final) − x(initial) = (−10 m) − (+10 m) = −20 m. This equals A's value, (5.0 − 25) m = −20 m: displacement is a change in position, so it does not depend on where the origin is placed. (Distance travelled = 70 m + 90 m = 160 m.)
items.specStatementText: the change in position is the displacement
items.working: According to B, positions are 15 m less than according to A: the runner starts at (25 − 15) m = +10 m and finishes at (5.0 − 15) m = −10 m. Displacement = x(final) − x(initial) = (−10 m) − (+10 m) = −20 m. This equals A's value, (5.0 − 25) m = −20 m: displacement is a change in position, so it does not depend on where the origin is placed. (Distance travelled = 70 m + 90 m = 160 m.)

items.q: A ball is thrown vertically upwards from a point 1.20 m above the ground. It rises to a maximum height of 6.70 m above the ground, falls, and is caught at a point 1.70 m above the ground. Upwards is taken as positive. What are the distance travelled by the ball and its displacement, from the throw to the catch?
items.correct: Distance 10.5 m; displacement +0.50 m
items.misconception: Distance 10.5 m; displacement +10.5 m
items.why:
In everyday use 'how far did you go' means the distance travelled, and in many introductory problems the body moves in one direction so the two values coincide. Students therefore treat the words as synonyms. Distance adds up every part of the path; displacement depends only on the start and end positions. A runner completing one lap of a track travels 400 m but has zero displacement.

Working: Distance travelled = length of path = (6.70 − 1.20) m up + (6.70 − 1.70) m down = 5.50 m + 5.00 m = 10.5 m. Displacement = change in position = (1.70 − 1.20) m = +0.50 m (0.50 m upwards).
items.specStatementText: the difference between distance and displacement
items.random_wrong: Distance 10.5 m; displacement +1.70 m

items.q: The graph shows how the velocity of a car varies with time during the first 10 s of its motion along a straight road. What is the displacement of the car during these 10 s?
items.why:
Students learn several motion graphs, each with a gradient and an area to interpret, often in quick succession. Confusion between area and gradient is a documented difficulty in research on students' interpretation of kinematics graphs. Check the units. Gradient = Δv/Δt has units m s⁻¹ ÷ s = m s⁻², an acceleration. Area = velocity × time has units m s⁻¹ × s = m, a displacement.

Working: Displacement = area under the velocity–time graph. Triangle from 0 to 4.0 s: ½ × 4.0 s × 20 m s⁻¹ = 40 m. Rectangle from 4.0 s to 10 s: 6.0 s × 20 m s⁻¹ = 120 m. Total displacement = 40 m + 120 m = 160 m.
items.specStatementText: velocity is the rate of change of position, and acceleration is the rate of change of velocity

items.q: The graph shows how the position x of a body moving along a straight line varies with time t. O, A, B and C are points on the graph. Which statement about the motion is correct?
items.correct: During BC the body moves at constant velocity in the negative direction.
items.misconception: During BC the body slows down, because the line slopes downwards.
items.why: Students read a motion graph as a picture of the motion, so 'going down' is read as 'losing speed'. Treating the slope of a position–time graph as a change in speed rather than as the velocity is a documented difficulty in research on students' interpretation of kinematics graphs. Ask what the gradient of the graph is. A straight sloping line has a constant gradient, so the velocity is constant: the sign of the gradient gives the direction of motion, and only a curve (changing gradient) shows a changing speed.
items.specStatementText: velocity is the rate of change of position, and acceleration is the rate of change of velocity
items.random_wrong: During AB the body moves at a constant velocity of 6 m s⁻¹.

items.q: The graph shows how the velocity of a body moving along a straight line varies with time. The dashed line is the tangent to the curve at P, where t = 2.0 s. What is the instantaneous acceleration of the body at t = 2.0 s?
items.correct: 2.0 m s⁻²
items.misconception: 6.0 m s⁻²
items.why:
Reading a value off a graph is the first graph skill students learn, and it is easier than finding a gradient. Confusing the slope of a graph with its height is a documented difficulty in research on students' interpretation of kinematics graphs. Identify what is plotted. On a position–time graph the height is a position and the gradient is a velocity; on a velocity–time graph the height is a velocity and the gradient is an acceleration.

Working: Instantaneous acceleration = gradient of the tangent to the velocity–time graph at P. The tangent passes through (0, 2.0 m s⁻¹) and (5.0 s, 12 m s⁻¹): a = (12 − 2.0) m s⁻¹ ÷ (5.0 − 0) s = 10 m s⁻¹ ÷ 5.0 s = 2.0 m s⁻². (For comparison, the average acceleration over the first 2.0 s is 6.0 m s⁻¹ ÷ 2.0 s = 3.0 m s⁻².)
items.specStatementText: the difference between instantaneous and average values of velocity, speed and acceleration, and how to determine them
items.random_wrong: 3.0 m s⁻²

items.q: The graph shows how the velocity of a body moving along a straight line varies with time. What is the displacement of the body between t = 0 and t = 4.0 s?
items.why:
In many first examples every quantity points the same way, so signs never matter. Students then enter magnitudes by habit, for example writing a braking deceleration as +4.0 m s⁻², or entering a downward launch velocity as positive when upwards is positive. Choose a positive direction at the start of every problem and give each vector the sign that matches its direction. A deceleration of a body moving in the positive direction is a negative acceleration.

Working: From the graph, u = +12 m s⁻¹, v = −4.0 m s⁻¹ at t = 4.0 s. The line is straight, so the acceleration is uniform and s = ((u + v)/2)t = ((12 + (−4.0))/2) × 4.0 = 4.0 m s⁻¹ × 4.0 s = 16 m. Check by areas: +½ × 3.0 × 12 = +18 m above the axis, −½ × 1.0 × 4.0 = −2.0 m below it, total +16 m. (a = (−4.0 − 12)/4.0 = −4.0 m s⁻²; s = ut + ½at² = 48 − 32 = 16 m.)
items.specStatementText: the equations of motion for solving problems with uniformly accelerated motion as given by s = ((u + v)/2)t; v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as

items.q: The graph shows how the acceleration of a dragster moving along a straight track varies with time. The dragster starts from rest at t = 0. What is the velocity of the dragster at t = 15 s?
items.correct: 80 m s⁻¹
items.misconception: 120 m s⁻¹
items.why:
Textbook problems for these equations are almost all in a straight line, so students remember 'straight line' as the condition and forget 'constant acceleration'. Check that the acceleration is constant before choosing an equation of motion. If it varies, use the motion graphs instead: the displacement is the area under the velocity–time graph and the acceleration is its gradient.

Working: Change in velocity = area under the acceleration–time graph. Rectangle from 0 to 5.0 s: 8.0 m s⁻² × 5.0 s = 40 m s⁻¹. Triangle from 5.0 s to 15 s: ½ × 10 s × 8.0 m s⁻² = 40 m s⁻¹. Starting from rest, v = 40 + 40 = 80 m s⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: motion with uniform and non-uniform acceleration

items.q: The diagram shows the path of a ball launched from O over level ground. Fluid resistance is negligible. P, Q and R are three points on the path. Which statement about the ball is correct?
items.correct: The speed of the ball at R is equal to the speed of the ball at P.
items.misconception: The horizontal component of velocity at R is less than at P.
items.why: The impetus idea, that a thrown body carries a force that dies away, is one of the most widely documented intuitive beliefs about motion. Everyday objects do slow down horizontally, because of fluid resistance, which reinforces it. A horizontal velocity changes only if there is a horizontal acceleration. Without fluid resistance the only acceleration is g, vertically downwards, so the horizontal component at the highest point equals the horizontal component at launch.

items.q: The graph shows how the velocity of a small ball released from rest varies with time. Curve P is for the ball falling in air. Line Q is for the same ball falling with fluid resistance negligible. Which statement about the graph is correct?
items.correct: At t = 0 the gradient of P equals the gradient of Q, as the fluid resistance is zero at release.
items.misconception: Once P becomes horizontal the ball in air is at rest, as its velocity has stopped changing.
items.why:
Students meet position–time graphs first, where a horizontal line does mean rest, and they read later graphs as pictures of the motion rather than checking which quantity is plotted. Read the axis label before interpreting a shape. A horizontal line on a velocity–time graph at 11 m s⁻¹ shows a body moving steadily at 11 m s⁻¹.

Working: Gradient of a velocity–time graph = acceleration. At t = 0 the ball is at rest, so the fluid resistance (which depends on speed) is zero and the acceleration is g for both cases: P and Q start with the same gradient, g. As the ball in air gains speed the fluid resistance grows, the resultant force and acceleration fall, and P curves below Q, becoming horizontal (zero acceleration, constant velocity) at the terminal speed.

items.q: A ball is thrown vertically upwards in air and falls back. The graph shows how its velocity varies with time, with upwards taken as positive; the ball reaches its highest point at t₁. Which statement about the motion is correct?
items.correct: The acceleration has a larger magnitude before t₁, as the graph is steeper there.
items.misconception: The acceleration is g throughout, as fluid resistance changes only the speed.
items.why: The phrase 'air resistance slows things down' is the usual first description, and students are taught that all bodies fall with acceleration g, so they keep g and treat fluid resistance as a separate slowing effect. Any change in how fast a body gains speed is a change in its acceleration. With fluid resistance, a falling body's acceleration starts at g and decreases towards zero, and a projectile's path becomes shorter, lower and lopsided.

items.q: Must a body move in the direction of its acceleration?
items.correct: No. A body moves in the direction of its velocity. Its acceleration can point in any direction relative to its velocity, including the opposite direction.
items.misconception: A body always moves in the direction of its acceleration.
items.why: Students link acceleration to the push or pull acting on a body and hold the intuitive belief that motion follows the push, the same intuition that makes them think a moving body must have a force in its direction of motion. Everyday examples, such as a car accelerating forwards, reinforce it. Velocity gives the direction of motion; acceleration gives the direction in which the velocity is changing. A ball thrown upwards moves up while its acceleration is downwards, and a braking car moves forwards while its acceleration is backwards.

items.q: Does a body with a larger speed have a larger acceleration?
items.correct: No. Acceleration measures how quickly the velocity changes, not how large the velocity is. A car cruising at a steady 30 m s⁻¹ has zero acceleration.
items.misconception: Acceleration increases when speed increases: a faster body has a greater acceleration, and a body whose speed is still rising has an increasing acceleration.
items.why: In everyday language 'acceleration' and 'speed' are both used for 'going fast', and students conflate a quantity with its rate of change. Research on students' understanding of acceleration repeatedly finds this velocity–acceleration confusion. Acceleration is the gradient of the velocity–time graph, not its height. The speed of a body can be rising while its acceleration is decreasing (a sprinter approaching top speed) or constant (free fall).

items.q: Can a displacement be negative?
items.correct: Yes. Displacement is a vector; in one dimension its sign shows its direction relative to the chosen positive direction.
items.misconception: Displacement is a length, so, like distance, it is always positive.
items.why: Students first meet lengths and distances, which cannot be negative, and 'displacement' is often introduced as 'distance in a straight line', so its direction is dropped. A displacement has a magnitude and a direction. With positive taken to the right, a body that ends 50 m to the left of where it started has displacement −50 m; the minus sign is information, not an error.

items.q: How is the gradient of a graph calculated?
items.correct: Gradient = change in the quantity on the vertical axis ÷ change in the quantity on the horizontal axis.
items.misconception: The gradient can be found by dividing the change along the horizontal axis by the change along the vertical axis.
items.why: The phrase 'rise over run' is easily reversed, and the correct order is a memorised convention rather than something students check with units. Divide the vertical change by the horizontal change and check the units: on a position–time graph Δx/Δt has units m s⁻¹, a velocity; Δt/Δx has units s m⁻¹, which is not a velocity.

items.q: In s = ut + ½at², can the ½ be dropped?
items.correct: No. The ½ is part of the equation: it arises because, under uniform acceleration from u, the average velocity over time t is u + ½at.
items.misconception: The displacement due to the acceleration is at², so s = ut + at² (for a drop from rest, s = gt²).
items.why: The equation is memorised as a string of symbols, and the ½ is the easiest part to lose. Students who have seen v = at and s = vt combine them into s = at² without averaging the velocity. Write the equation out in full each time: s = ut + ½at². For a body starting from rest, the displacement in time t is ½at², because its average velocity during that time is half its final velocity.

items.q: In ½at², which quantity is squared?
items.correct: The time. The term is ½ × a × t², with the time squared and the acceleration not.
items.misconception: The term ½at² means ½ × a × t, or the square is applied carelessly, so t is not squared.
items.why: Under time pressure, students substitute into the equation term by term and lose the index on t, especially when using a calculator without brackets. Substitute with brackets: ½ × a × (t)². A quick unit check helps: a × t has units m s⁻¹, a velocity, not a displacement; a × t² has units m.

items.q: Without fluid resistance, does a heavier body fall with a greater acceleration?
items.correct: No. In the absence of fluid resistance all bodies fall with the same acceleration, g, whatever their mass.
items.misconception: Heavier bodies fall faster than lighter ones, even when fluid resistance is negligible.
items.why: In everyday experience light objects such as feathers and paper fall slowly because fluid resistance affects them strongly, and a heavier body does experience a greater gravitational force. Students infer that the acceleration also depends on mass; this Aristotelian belief is widely documented. A body of twice the mass has twice the weight but also twice the mass to accelerate, so its acceleration is the same, g. Differences in everyday falling are caused by fluid resistance, not by mass itself.

items.q: Does a velocity–time graph have the same shape as the acceleration–time graph for the same motion?
items.correct: No. The acceleration is the gradient of the velocity–time graph, not its shape. A decreasing positive acceleration gives a velocity–time graph that rises ever less steeply, curving downwards (flattening off).
items.misconception: The shape of the velocity–time graph copies the shape of the acceleration–time graph, so a decreasing acceleration that levels off gives a velocity–time curve that bends upwards in the same way.
items.why: Students read kinematic graphs as pictures of the motion and carry the curvature of one graph over to the next, instead of linking the gradient of one graph to the height of the other; this graph-as-picture, shape-copying difficulty is well documented in research on students' interpretation of kinematics graphs. Read the height of the acceleration–time graph as the gradient of the velocity–time graph. If the acceleration is large at first and then smaller, the velocity–time graph is steep at first and then flatter, so it curves downwards even while the acceleration graph curves upwards.
